summary: Discusses some unusual interface problems in connecting an Illinois plasma terminal, the Plato terminal, to the ARPANET.

plainLanguage.summary: A special glowing screen from one university was hard to connect to the network. This note talks about the odd problems that came up.

questions: how to connect special terminals to networks
subtitle: Connecting a plasma display terminal to the ARPANET

tldr.problem: Illinois PLATO plasma display terminals were expensive to connect remotely using long-distance telephone lines, and their non-standard communication protocol made ARPANET access difficult.
tldr.mechanism: Engineers designed a two-mode interface adapter that allows the terminal to operate in ASCII mode for standard network access, or in PLATO mode for compatibility with the existing PLATO system, bridging the gap between the terminal's native protocol and network standards.
tldr.outcome: The interface allowed PLATO terminals to connect via the ARPANET as a cost-effective alternative to long-distance phone lines, with plans for a more flexible microcomputer-based version.

today: RFC 600 is an historical account of work done at UCSB in 1973 to adapt an Illinois PLATO terminal for ARPANET use. The PLATO system itself is now obsolete, but the problem it addressed—connecting specialized terminals with non-standard protocols to general networks—remains relevant to modern terminal emulation and protocol bridging.

sections.title: The PLATO System and Its Terminal
sections.content:
The PLATO IV System at the University of Illinois was a sophisticated computer-aided instruction platform with a unique plasma display terminal: a glowing screen that displayed information in ways most computer terminals could not. The terminal could show graphics and had specialized capabilities for education applications.

However, connecting PLATO terminals over long distances required expensive long-distance telephone lines running at slow speeds. Since ARPA had already built the ARPANET as a cost-effective national network, the obvious solution was to connect these terminals through the network instead.
sections.plainLanguage: There was a special glowing computer screen for teaching that was hard to connect to faraway computers. Scientists wanted to use the cheaper network instead of expensive phone calls.

sections.title: The Two-Mode Interface
sections.content:
The plasma terminal naturally sent and received data using Frequency Shift Keying (FSK) modulation over phone lines: 1200 bits per second in full-duplex mode on dedicated lines, or slower split speeds (1200 bits/sec receiving, 120 bits/sec sending) on dial-up.

To work with the ARPANET and its network nodes (called TIPs), the terminal needed to speak a different language: standard ASCII codes. The solution was to build an interface that could operate in two modes. In ASCII mode, it would send and receive standard 8-bit ASCII characters for normal network access, losing graphics capability. In PLATO mode, it could embed PLATO's proprietary data in 8-bit codes to pass transparently through the network while maintaining full functionality.

One challenge was preventing network nodes from misinterpreting PLATO codes. For example, the @ symbol is a TIP command prefix, so the interface had to escape or omit such codes to avoid accidental command triggers.
sections.plainLanguage: The interface was like a translator that could switch between two languages: network language (ASCII) for regular network use, and PLATO language when talking to the PLATO system. It had to be careful not to let special codes trick the network.

sections.title: From Hardware to Flexible Software
sections.content:
The prototype interface built at UCSB in 1973 used dedicated hardware and provided the two-mode switching, though it sacrificed some capabilities in ASCII mode (it could only display 124 out of 128 ASCII characters).

Looking ahead, the team recognized that a fixed hardware solution was too rigid. They planned to replace it with a microcomputer-based interface, complete with ROM storage for the control program. This approach would let the interface be reprogrammed to emulate other terminal types, implement cursors, and eventually support network graphics protocols without replacing the hardware itself.
sections.plainLanguage: The first version was hardwired, but the team realized they could use a small computer instead. That way, they could reprogram it to do new tricks later without building new hardware.
